newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Police end violent pay strikes in parts of Brazil.
newsitem.headline: Police end violent pay strikes in parts of Brazil.

text.p: Brazilian police have ended a strike for better pay in two northeastern states on Thursday after several days of violent clashes with special military police units and army troops, an official said.

"It's all over," military police Capt. Franco Neto told Reuters from Fortaleza, capital of Ceara state. "There were few absentees but those that were absent have returned. There were no repercussions and no deal was struck."
In the state of Alagoas, police also ended a 15-day strike and returned to work on Thursday afternoon after the state government agreed to gradually pay officers months' worth of back wages.
Police in several other states remained on strike.

Eight strike leaders and 23 striking police officers were arrested on Thursday in Fortaleza, two days after a bloody gun-battle between striking police and on-duty officers, Globo television reported.
Up to six people were injured when officers on both sides of the dispute traded shots.
A further 96 officers were dismissed and will shortly be replaced by reserve army troops as part of a plan to restore discipline in the troubled region, Globo added.
President Fernando Henrique Cardoso on Wednesday called rebel officers "deserters" and pledged not to give in to their demands.
"This was an uprising. These people are deserters," a presidential spokewoman quoted Cardoso as saying. "This is not a strike. People with guns in their hands have no right to strike."

While he recognised that police wages -- often as low as $250 per month -- were a problem, the president said he would not tolerate further breakdown of discipline, the spokeswoman said. Cardoso made the comments to state-run television network Radiobras while visiting a navy warship.

Several times in the last few weeks, police protests for better wages have ended in gunbattles. In June an on-duty officer was killed by a bullet fired during a protest. Army troops have patrolled at least three cities to keep order.

The violent demonstrations have brought to a head the long-standing problem of Brazil's notorious police force. When police officers were filmed beating and shooting at residents of a Sao Paulo shanty-town in April, Cardoso reacted by ordering a reform of the institution.
But officials rule out any quick move to break the autonomy of the country's military police, a step which human rights groups say is essential to ending brutality.
